"-아/어 주다" also becomes "-아/어 드리다". In restaurants and shops you often hear "해 드릴게요" and "가져다드리겠습니다".
dl: Manager, I have something to tell you.
to give (humble) (드릴 말씀 = something to tell you)
May I ask you something about vacation?
Of course. Give the application form to me.

sm: 내가 윗사람에게 하는 일은 "드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다, 모시다, 말씀드리다"로 말합니다.
For your actions toward older or higher people, use "드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다, 모시다, 말씀드리다".

i: 윗사람과 관계있는 것을 말할 때 쓰는 높임 명사입니다.
These are honorific nouns used when talking about things related to older or higher people.
w: May I know the name of the person in charge?
May I ask how old you are?
I went to the boss's house.
I was invited to the boss's house.
Excuse me, may I ask something?
I've heard a lot about you.
That is the new factory manager.
tp: 높임 명사를 쓰면 동사도 높입니다. "이름이 뭐예요?"(보통) "성함이 어떻게 되세요?"(높임).
If you use an honorific noun, use an honorific verb too. "이름이 뭐예요?" (normal), "성함이 어떻게 되세요?" (honorific).
"진지"는 집안 어른께 쓰는 말이고, 일터와 가게에서는 "식사"를 씁니다. "식사하셨어요?"는 한국의 인사말입니다.
"진지" is used for elders in the family; at work and in shops use "식사". "식사하셨어요?" (Have you eaten?) is a Korean greeting.
dl: Welcome. May I have your name?
I'm Park Minha. I came to see Manager Kim.
네, 과장님께 말씀드리겠습니다. 이쪽에서 잠시만 기다려 주십시오.
Yes, I'll let the manager know. Please wait here for a moment.
ne, gwajangnimkke malsseumdeurigesseumnida ijjogeseo jamsiman gidaryeo jusipssio
sm: 이름 → 성함, 나이 → 연세, 집 → 댁, 밥 → 식사, 말 → 말씀, 사람 → 분.
이름 → 성함, 나이 → 연세, 집 → 댁, 밥 → 식사, 말 → 말씀, 사람 → 분.

i: Korean shows respect to the listener by using a humble word for "I". English has no humble "I", so practice "저" carefully.
Korean shows respect to the listener by using a humble word for "I". English has no humble form of "I", so practice "저" carefully.
w: to do wrong, to make a mistake
I'll give you my phone number.
Our team is on the night shift today.
tp: "-요"나 "-습니다"로 말할 때는 "저"를 씁니다. "나는 샘입니다"는 어색합니다.
When you speak with "-요" or "-습니다", use "저". "나는 샘입니다" sounds strange.
"저가"가 아니라 "제가", "나가"가 아니라 "내가"입니다.
It is "제가", not "저가", and "내가", not "나가".
손님에게 회사나 가게를 말할 때 "저희 회사, 저희 가게"라고 합니다. 그러나 나라는 낮추지 않고 "우리나라"라고 합니다.
When you talk about your company or shop to customers, say "저희 회사, 저희 가게". But you don't lower your country; say "우리나라".
dl: 누가 이 일을 할 수 있어요?
nuga i ireul hal su isseoyo?
Our team can do it together.
sm: 윗사람 앞에서는 "나, 내가, 내, 우리" 대신 "저, 제가, 제, 저희"를 씁니다.
In front of older or higher people, use "저, 제가, 제, 저희" instead of "나, 내가, 내, 우리".

i: 한국어는 같은 인사도 상대에 따라 세 가지 말씨로 합니다. 격식(-습니다), 부드러운 높임(-요), 반말입니다.
In Korean, the same greeting has three speech styles depending on the listener: formal (-습니다), soft polite (-요) and casual (반말).
w: Hello. I'm Sam, and I start working here today.
Hello. Nice to meet you. (first meeting)
안녕하세요? 이 층에 새로 이사 왔어요.
annyeonghaseyo? i cheunge saero isa wasseoyo
Hello. I just moved to this floor.
Thank you so much for interpreting.
Thank you for lending me the umbrella.
I'm sorry. I won't be late again.
Sorry. I couldn't answer the phone.
tp: English "hello" is the same for everyone, but in Korean the form changes with the listener. If you don't know which to use, use "-요".
English "hello" is the same for everyone, but in Korean the form changes with the listener. If you are not sure which to use, use "-요".
윗사람에게 "미안해요, 고마워요"는 가볍게 들립니다. "죄송합니다, 감사합니다"를 씁니다.
To older or higher people, "미안해요, 고마워요" sounds too light. Use "죄송합니다, 감사합니다".
"안녕"은 만날 때와 헤어질 때 다 쓰지만 친구와 아이에게만 씁니다.
"안녕" is used both when meeting and when leaving, but only with friends and children.
dl: 아, 샘 씨. 안녕하세요? 일은 할 만해요?
Oh, Sam. Hello. Is the work okay for you?
a, saem ssi annyeonghaseyo? ireun hal manhaeyo?
Sam, hi! Did you have lunch?
sm: 인사는 격식 "-습니다", 부드러운 "-요", 반말 세 단계가 있습니다.
Greetings have three levels: formal "-습니다", soft "-요", and casual.

i: 묻는 말도 세 가지 말씨가 있습니다. 듣는 사람이 윗사람이면 "-(으)시-"도 넣습니다.
Questions also have three speech styles. If the listener is older or higher, also add "-(으)시-".
w: Where are you going? I'll take you there.
Sir, where are you going? Shall I get the car ready?
Team leader, where are you going?
Where are you going at this hour?
It's your day off. Where are you going?
Where are you going? Let's go together.
Where are you going after work?
Team leader, have you eaten? Would you like to go together?
Did you eat? Want to eat together?
Did you eat? Shall I make ramyeon?
Are you sick? Are you okay?
Did you fall? Are you okay?
You don't look well. Are you okay?
tp: 윗사람이 하는 일을 물을 때는 말끝만 바꾸지 않고 "-(으)시-"를 넣습니다. "어디 가요?"가 아니라 "어디 가세요?"입니다.
When you ask about what an older or higher person does, don't just change the ending; add "-(으)시-". Say "어디 가세요?", not "어디 가요?".
"어디 가세요?", "식사하셨어요?"는 인사입니다. 자세히 대답하지 않아도 됩니다. "네, 잠깐 나가요", "네, 먹었습니다".
"어디 가세요?" and "식사하셨어요?" are greetings. You don't need to answer in detail: "네, 잠깐 나가요", "네, 먹었습니다".
dl: I'm going to the warehouse. Where are you going, team leader?
To the office. Did you have lunch?
Yes, I did. Have you eaten, team leader?
sm: 윗사람에게 물을 때는 "-(으)세요?"나 "-(으)십니까?"를 씁니다.
When you ask older or higher people, use "-(으)세요?" or "-(으)십니까?".
qz: 사장님에게 맞는 말은? 어디 가? / 어디 가십니까?
반장님이 "밥 먹었어?"라고 물었습니다. 맞는 대답은? 응, 먹었어 / 네, 먹었습니다

i: 부탁하거나 시키는 말도 세 가지 말씨가 있습니다. 부탁은 공손할수록 길어집니다.
Requests and instructions also have three speech styles. The more polite a request is, the longer it gets.
w: Could you say that again, please?
Could you close the window, please?
Could you say it again slowly, please?
Excuse me, but please help me.
I can't read this Korean document. Please help me.

tp: 윗사람에게 부탁할 때는 시키는 모양보다 묻는 모양이 더 공손합니다. "-아/어 주시겠어요?", "-아/어 주실 수 있으세요?"
When you ask an older or higher person, a question form is more polite than an order form: "-아/어 주시겠어요?", "-아/어 주실 수 있으세요?"
부탁 앞에 "죄송하지만", "실례지만", "바쁘시겠지만"을 붙이면 더 부드럽습니다.
Adding "죄송하지만", "실례지만" or "바쁘시겠지만" (I know you're busy, but…) before a request makes it softer.
dl: 과장님, 바쁘시겠지만 이 서류 좀 봐 주시겠어요?
Manager, I know you're busy, but could you look at this document?
gwajangnim, bappeusigejjiman i seoryu jom bwa jusigesseoyo?

There's no signature here. Sign it and bring it back.
to not have, there is no
yeogi seomyeongi eomneyo seomyeonghaeseo dasi gajeowayo
sm: 부탁은 "줘 → 주세요 → 주십시오 → 주시겠어요?" 순서로 공손해집니다.
Requests get more polite in this order: "줘 → 주세요 → 주십시오 → 주시겠어요?".

Answers also change with the speech style. At work, it is important to answer clearly.

No. I'm not the one who did it.
Yes, that's right. The contract details are correct.
tp: 윗사람에게 "응", "어"라고 대답하면 큰 실례입니다. 꼭 "네"나 "예"라고 합니다.
Answering an older or higher person with "응" or "어" is very rude. Always say "네" or "예".
못 알아들었는데 "네"라고 하지 않습니다. "죄송합니다. 잘 못 들었습니다", "다시 한번 말씀해 주십시오"라고 합니다. 일터에서 모르면서 "네"라고 하면 사고가 납니다.
Don't say "네" if you didn't understand. Say "죄송합니다. 잘 못 들었습니다" or "다시 한번 말씀해 주십시오". At work, saying "네" when you don't understand can cause accidents.
"네" means not only "yes" but also "I'm listening". It is also the answer when someone calls you: "샘 씨!" "네!"
"네" means not only "yes" but is also used to show "I'm listening". It is also the answer when someone calls your name: "샘 씨!" "네!"

To older or higher people answer "네, 알겠습니다"; if you didn't understand, say "잘 못 들었습니다".

i: 같은 뜻의 말을 듣는 사람에 따라 바꾸는 연습입니다. 말씨는 나이, 직급, 친한 정도로 정합니다.
This is practice changing words with the same meaning for different listeners. The speech style depends on age, job rank and how close you are.

good work (said to someone younger or lower)

I have to come to work early tomorrow, so I'll be going now.

It's time for my bus, so I'll go first.
I'm tired, so I'm going first.
I'm younger, so please speak casually to me.

You're older than me, so please speak casually.
tp: 처음 만난 사람에게는 나이와 관계없이 "-요"를 씁니다. 반말은 상대가 "말 편하게 해요"라고 한 뒤에 씁니다.
With people you meet for the first time, use "-요" whatever their age. Use casual speech only after the other person says "말 편하게 해요".
한국 일터에서는 나이보다 직급과 먼저 들어온 순서가 앞섭니다. 나이가 어려도 선배와 상사에게는 높임말을 씁니다.
At Korean workplaces, job rank and who joined first matter more than age. Even if they are younger, use polite speech with seniors and bosses.
dl: Manager, I'll be going now. Thank you for your hard work.
(먼저 가 보겠습니다 = I'll leave first, said when leaving before others)
to work hard (수고하셨습니다 = thank you for your hard work)

to work hard (수고하셨습니다 = thank you for your hard work)

sm: 상사와 손님에게는 격식, 동료에게는 "-요", 친한 친구에게만 반말을 씁니다.
Use the formal style with bosses and customers, "-요" with coworkers, and casual speech only with close friends.

hyeong, da-eum dare gachi nepal gallae?

(보고 싶다 = to miss, want to see)

tp: 영어와 달리 한국어는 가족이 아닌 친한 윗사람도 "형, 오빠, 누나, 언니"라고 부릅니다. 일터에서도 친해지면 "형"이라고 부릅니다.
Unlike English, Korean uses "형, 오빠, 누나, 언니" for close older people who are not family. At work, too, people say "형" when they become close.
"아빠, 엄마"는 아이나 친한 사이에서 쓰는 말이고, 남에게 말할 때는 "아버지, 어머니"가 점잖습니다.
"아빠, 엄마" are used by children or between close people. When talking to others, "아버지, 어머니" sounds more polite.
동생은 이름으로 부릅니다. "동생!" 하고 부르지 않습니다. 이름 뒤에 "아/야"를 붙입니다. "민하야", "샘아".
Call younger siblings by name. Don't call "동생!". Add "아/야" after the name: "민하야", "샘아".
dl: Sam, how many brothers and sisters do you have?

Men say "형, 누나"; women say "오빠, 언니".

tp: 윗사람을 "이름 + 씨"로 부르면 큰 실례입니다. "김 씨", "민하 씨"가 아니라 "김 과장님", "반장님"이라고 부릅니다.
Calling an older or higher person "name + 씨" is very rude. Don't say "김 씨" or "민하 씨"; say "김 과장님", "반장님".
한국 이름은 성이 앞에 옵니다. "김민하"에서 "김"이 성이고 "민하"가 이름입니다. 직함은 성 뒤에 붙입니다.
In Korean names, the family name comes first. In "김민하", "김" is the family name and "민하" is the given name. Job titles go after the family name.

tp: 가장 안전한 말은 "저기요"와 "여기요"입니다. 누구에게나 쓸 수 있습니다. 식당에서 직원을 부를 때는 "여기요"입니다.
The safest words are "저기요" and "여기요". You can use them with anyone. To call staff in a restaurant, say "여기요".
"아줌마"는 낮추는 느낌이 있어서 "아주머니"나 "이모님", "사장님"을 씁니다. 젊은 여자에게 "아주머니"라고 하면 기분 나빠합니다.
"아줌마" can sound rude, so use "아주머니", "이모님" or "사장님". Young women don't like being called "아주머니".
가게 주인은 남자든 여자든 "사장님"이라고 부르면 좋아합니다.
Shop owners, men or women, like being called "사장님".
dl: Yes, what can I get you?
이모님, 된장찌개 하나하고 공깃밥 하나 주세요.
Auntie, one doenjang jjigae and one bowl of rice, please.
imonim, doenjangjjigae hanahago gonggitppap hana juseyo
Okay, I'll bring it right away.
sm: 모르는 사람은 "저기요", 식당에서는 "여기요", 가게 주인은 "사장님"이라고 부릅니다.
Call strangers "저기요", staff in restaurants "여기요", and shop owners "사장님".

i: An action a person does (문을 열다) and something that happens by itself (문이 열리다) use different words. English uses "open" for both, but Korean has a pair.
An action a person does (문을 열다) and something that happens by itself (문이 열리다) use different words. English uses "open" for both, but Korean has a pair.
w: It smells, so please open the window.
to open (by itself), to be opened
The door opens when you touch your card.
Close the door when you go out.
Close the door when you turn on the air conditioner.
to close (by itself), to be closed
The door closed because of the wind.
엘리베이터 문이 닫힐 때 손을 넣지 마세요.
ellibe-iteo muni datil ttae soneul neochi maseyo
Don't put your hand in when the elevator door is closing.
If it's dark, turn on your phone's flashlight.
to turn on (by itself), to come on
If the warning light comes on, stop the machine.
Turn off the lights when you leave work.
I turn off the light before I go to sleep.
Be sure to turn off the electric blanket when you go out.
to go off, to go out (light, machine)
The battery ran out, so my phone turned off.
to not have, there is no
x: open the door ↔ the door opens
close the door ↔ the door closes
turn on the light ↔ the light comes on
turn off the light ↔ the light goes out
tp: 조사로 가립니다. 사람이 하는 일은 "을/를", 저절로 되는 것은 "이/가"입니다. "문을 열어요", "문이 열려요".
The particle shows the difference. For what a person does, use "을/를"; for what happens by itself, use "이/가": "문을 열어요", "문이 열려요".
고장을 알릴 때는 저절로 되는 쪽 동사를 씁니다. "문이 안 열려요", "기계가 안 켜져요", "불이 안 꺼져요".
When you report a problem, use the "by itself" verb: "문이 안 열려요", "기계가 안 켜져요", "불이 안 꺼져요".
dl: Team leader, the warehouse door won't open.
Did you open it with the key?
네, 열쇠로 열어 봤는데 안 열립니다.
Yes, I tried with the key, but it won't open.
ne, yeolsoero yeoreo bwanneunde an yeollimnida
Really? Are the lights on inside?
sm: 사람이 하면 "을/를 열다", 저절로 되면 "이/가 열리다"입니다.
If a person does it, "을/를 열다"; if it happens by itself, "이/가 열리다".

i: 물건이 깨지고 끊어지고 떨어지는 것을 말할 때, 누가 그랬는지와 저절로 그렇게 됐는지를 가려 말합니다.
When things break, snap or fall, Korean shows whether someone did it or it happened by itself.
w: I broke a plate. I'm sorry.
I broke a bowl while washing the dishes.
Wrap broken glass in newspaper and throw it away.
to cut, to hang up, to quit
Since I quit drinking, I'm saving money.
to break, to be cut off
The internet went down, so I can't make the call.
I dropped my phone in the toilet.
Please fix my room's door handle.
tp: 잘못을 알릴 때는 "제가 ~을/를 ~했습니다"라고 솔직하게 말합니다. "제가 부품을 떨어뜨렸습니다. 죄송합니다."
When you report a mistake, say it honestly: "제가 ~을/를 ~했습니다". "제가 부품을 떨어뜨렸습니다. 죄송합니다."
누가 그랬는지 모르거나 저절로 된 일은 "~이/가 ~졌습니다"라고 합니다. "유리가 깨져 있었습니다."
When you don't know who did it, or it happened by itself, say "~이/가 ~졌습니다": "유리가 깨져 있었습니다." (The glass was already broken.)
dl: 반장님, 죄송합니다. 제가 부품 상자를 떨어뜨렸습니다.
Team leader, I'm sorry. I dropped a box of parts.
banjangnim, joesonghamnida jega bupum sangjareul tteoreotteuryeosseumnida
to not have, there is no
네, 괜찮습니다. 그런데 부품 두 개가 깨졌습니다.
No, I'm okay. But two parts broke.
ne, gwaenchansseumnida geureonde bupum du gaega kkaejeosseumnida
알았어요. 바로 말해 줘서 고마워요. 다음부터 조심해요.
Okay. Thanks for telling me right away. Be careful next time.
arasseoyo baro malhae jwoseo gomawoyo da-eumbuteo josimhaeyo
sm: 내가 했으면 "깼어요, 떨어뜨렸어요", 저절로 됐으면 "깨졌어요, 떨어졌어요"입니다.
If you did it, "깼어요, 떨어뜨렸어요"; if it happened by itself, "깨졌어요, 떨어졌어요".

i: 일을 시작하고 끝내는 말도 사람이 하는 것과 저절로 되는 것이 짝을 이룹니다.
Words for starting and ending also come in pairs: what a person does and what happens by itself.
w: I start the night shift next week.
When the rainy season starts, it gets very humid.
Finish cleaning up, then leave work.
What time does the class end?
When my contract ends, I'll go back to my hometown.
I changed my money into dollars.
I changed my phone plan to a cheaper one.
다음 달부터 통근 버스 시간이 바뀌어요.
da-eum dalbuteo tonggeun beoseu sigani bakkwieoyo
The commuter bus times will change from next month.
Did you decide where to travel?
We decide our vacation dates together with coworkers.
The date of the team dinner has been decided.
When your date for going home is decided, let me know.
tp: "몇 시에 끝나요?"는 일이 끝나는 때를 묻고, "몇 시까지 끝내요?"는 내가 끝내야 하는 때를 묻습니다.
"몇 시에 끝나요?" asks when the work ends; "몇 시까지 끝내요?" asks by when you have to finish it.
공지와 안내는 저절로 되는 쪽 동사를 많이 씁니다. "근무 시간이 바뀌었습니다", "휴일이 정해졌습니다". 누가 정했는지는 말하지 않습니다.
Notices and announcements often use the "by itself" verbs: "근무 시간이 바뀌었습니다", "휴일이 정해졌습니다". They don't say who decided.
dl: 반장님, 오늘 일은 몇 시에 끝납니까?
Team leader, what time does work end today?
banjangnim, oneul ireun myeot sie kkeunnamnikka?
원래 여섯 시인데 오늘은 시간이 바뀌었어요. 여덟 시에 끝나요.
Usually at six, but the time changed today. We finish at eight.
wollae yeoseot siinde oneureun sigani bakkwieosseoyo yeodeol sie kkeunnayo
By when do I have to finish this work?
sm: 사람이 하면 "시작하다, 끝내다, 바꾸다", 저절로 되면 "시작되다, 끝나다, 바뀌다"입니다.
If a person does it, "시작하다, 끝내다, 바꾸다"; if it happens by itself, "시작되다, 끝나다, 바뀌다".
